thread.title: Lenovo Now Getting A Fairer Assessment From Investors - Lenovo Group Ltd. ADR (OTCMKTS:LNVGY)

author: Stephen Simpson, CFA
title: Lenovo Now Getting A Fairer Assessment From Investors - Lenovo Group Ltd. ADR (OTCMKTS:LNVGY)
text:
Two out of three isn’t bad. Lenovo ( OTCPK:LNVGY ) appears to be having some ongoing success in rejuvenating its PC business, while its server/data center business continues to grow on the back of its SDI and hyperscale efforts. Mobile is still a challenge, but the company has seen some shipment growth improvement in North America and has had some success with stripping costs out of this business.
Lenovo’s improving performance hasn’t gone unnoticed, and even with a sharp dive connected to worries about Chinese-government sponsored “hacking”, Lenovo has outperformed many of its consumer tech peers like Apple ( AAPL ) and HP ( HPQ ) since my last update on the company. While expectations are still relatively low for Lenovo, I don’t see the valuation as so unreasonable anymore, and I believe the next leg in the company’s performance will have to be driven by better margin performance in the non-PC operations.
Decent Results, Boosted By A Non-Operating Gain Lenovo’s fiscal second quarter (calendar third quarter) results certainly weren’t bad, and the company continues to show progress in some important areas of the business, but it also wasn’t quite as strong as a cursory first glance might suggest.
Revenue rose 14% for the quarter, which was good for a 3% beat relative to expectations. Once again, the PC business led the outperformance, with 18% revenue growth on 12% shipment growth. Shipments would have been up around 6% on an organic basis (excluding the Fujitsu deal); still meaningfully better than the 1% market contraction in the quarter. Lenovo’s efforts to control costs and shift its mix up-market continue to pay off in margins, with the pre-tax income up 37% and margin up 70bp at the segment level.
The Data Center business delivered 58% revenue growth which was more or less in the range of sell-side expectations, but with good growth trends in SDI and hyperscale and some momentum with Microsoft ( MSFT ). Progress on margins appears to have stalled out, with another quarter of around $60 million in pre-tax losses; better than last year, but flattish for the third straight quarter.
Lenovo’s mobile business saw a 23% revenue drop as the company absorbs the impact of exiting markets where it was both uncompetitive and saw little future for itself. North American shipments were up strongly in the quarter (up 53%), taking Lenovo’s market share to a little less than 8% (#4), while the company held its #2 position in Latin America. The cost-cutting here continues to lead to better results, with the pre-tax loss down significantly from last year and roughly half of the first quarter’s level (and with a negative pre-tax margin of 3.1% on par with the server business).
At the corporate level, Lenovo’s gross margin was about 20 basis points shy of expectations. While the pre-tax line looked like it significantly outperformed expectations (by roughly one-third), the figure was boosted by a financial gain and the adjusted figure was basically in line with expectations as the company compensated for a lower gross margin with some progress in opex leverage.
And Now? Lenovo does seem to have some legitimate momentum in its PC business again. Moving up-market has certainly improved the company’s ASP performance, but that hasn’t compromised popularity. Lenovo’s strong volume in the third quarter allowed it to regain the top spot in the PC market, with almost 24% share versus HP’s 23% share, and it looks like Lenovo would have squeaked out ahead of HP even without the Fujitsu deal.
Looking ahead, the CPU shortage from Intel ( INTC ) is going to impact the next two quarters’ results, but management believes they can offset that somewhat with AMD ( AMD ) chips. Time will tell how customers respond to that, but I don’t see Lenovo as particularly disadvantaged relative to HP or Dell . As far as tariffs go, while management is monitoring the situation, the company has a lot of global manufacturing flexibility that can help offset tariffs at least in part.
It’s not as clear to me what happens next in the Data Center segment. A new partnership with NetApp ( NTAP ) won’t hurt, but there’s ongoing, if not increasing, competitive pressure from HP, Dell, and Huawei , as well as newer entrants. What’s more, maintaining gross margins is proving to be challenging given the pressures in the market and there’s only so far Lenovo can go with operating cost reductions before it bites into sales momentum. While Lenovo sold off a month ago on a Bloomberg report about servers from China including “spy chips” on their motherboards, Lenovo announced that it doesn’t use the supplier in question ( Super Micro (NASDAQ: SMCI )) and it reiterated that most of its servers sold in the U.S. are manufactured in Mexico.
The cost reductions in the Mobile business seem to be tracking well, but this too is a business with an uncertain future. I believe Lenovo will struggle to make worthwhile profits even at 10% share of the North American market, and growth across the market has slowed. On the other hand, Lenovo has shown it can make money in a thin-margin, more commodified PC business and the increasing competition among mobile components from new entrants (including Akoustis ( OTC:AKTS )) could allow Lenovo to replicate that successful cost-focused PC model.
The Opportunity Although Lenovo’s PC strategy has paid dividends and I think there could be some upside in both the data center and mobile businesses, it’s not going to get easier from here. I have once again modestly revised my revenue assumptions higher, driving my long-term estimated growth rate closer to 3%. I have also made some adjustments to my opex assumptions that drive a higher long-term average operating and FCF margin, with long-term FCF margins in the low 2%’s. All of that adds a little more than a $1/ADR to my fair value, and I’m still using a low double-digit discount rate that is higher than I normally use.
The Bottom Line Even after Lenovo’s outperformance, it does still appear priced for low double-digit total returns. That’s not bad, and it supports holding the shares, but I have a higher hurdle rate for recommending riskier stocks (and I believe Lenovo is riskier than average), so I’m a little more cautious about calling this a buy today. Investors and sell-side analysts seem to have come around at least a bit on this name, but there’s still pressure on management to drive better results in the coming quarters and expectations are certainly higher now.
Disclosure: I am/we are long LNVGY.
